newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Second Australian politician quits over shares.
newsitem.headline: Second Australian politician quits over shares.

text.p: Allegations of conflict of interest cost Australian Prime Minister John Howard a second member of his new government on Tuesday as the Labor opposition stepped up a campaign to remove a third.
Brian Gibson, parliamentary secretary to the treasurer, told parliament he would resign because a decision he made earlier in the year had benefited a company in which he held shares.

But the Labor opposition, which claimed the scalp of former assistant treasurer Jim Short over a similar issue on Sunday, was not satisfied and took aim at Industry Minister John Moore, one of the most senior members of the government.

"We have here an unequivocal case of circumstances in which a minister must resign," opposition industry spokesman Simon Crean told parliament, arguing that Moore had also made ministerial decisions that benefited his shareholdings.
Moore refuses to go, saying he had done nothing wrong and was trying to sell his shares.
Gibson said that in his case resignation was the only honourable course to take.

"These circumstance could be perceived to consitute a conflict of interest and my failure to act accordingly necessitates the action I have taken," he told parliament, emphasising he had intended no improper action.
Short quit as assistant treasurer on Sunday after his office discovered he had granted a banking license to a subsidiary of a bank in which he held shares.
"They didn't pay enough attention to the guidelines and each of them has paid a very heavy price," Howard said on radio.

The opposition has also criticised Treasurer Peter Costello over his wife's ownership of 200 shares in a major bank but the government has deflected the attacks by saying a married woman must have the right to manage her own affairs.
The loss of two members has been the biggest crisis the Liberal-National government has faced since its March landslide election win ended 13 years of Labor rule.
Howard moved to contain the damage by saying his ministerial code of conduct was too strict.
He now wanted ministers to be able to put their investments at arms length by placing them in the hands of a trustee.
"I don't want a situation where people who have decent share portfolios are afraid to go into politics," Howard said.
